Lend
LEND
v.t.
From Anglo-Saxon laenan, to grant for a time, from laen, a loan. Webster 1828: to grant to another for temporary use, on the express or implied condition that the thing shall be returned. The law of Israel bent the ordinary terms of lending toward the poor, and Christ removed them altogether.

Biblical Definition

The Mosaic law treats lending to a poor Israelite as an obligation rather than an opportunity: thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth (Deuteronomy 15:8) — and the surrounding verses forbid the calculation that the year of release is near. Interest is excluded outright in such a case: If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury (Exodus 22:25). The Psalter makes lending a mark of the righteous man rather than a risk he takes: He is ever merciful, and lendeth; and his seed is blessed (Psalm 37:26). Our Lord then removes the last remaining expectation: love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil (Luke 6:35). The ground given is not the borrower’s worthiness but the Father’s character, and the imitation is the point.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LEND as to grant to another for temporary use, on the express or implied condition that the thing shall be returned; to afford or grant; to permit to use for a time.

expand to see more

LEND, v.t. — To grant to another for temporary use, on the condition that the thing shall be returned; as, to lend a book.

To grant money for temporary use, usually on interest.

To afford; to grant; to furnish; as, to lend assistance.

To let for hire or compensation; as, to lend a horse.

Anglo-Saxon laenan, from laen, a loan — the root of English loan.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 15:8 — "But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth."

Exodus 22:25 — "If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury."

Psalm 37:26 — "He is ever merciful, and lendeth; and his seed is blessed."

Luke 6:35 — "But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil."

Modern Corruption

Luke 6:35 commands lending without expectation of return, and its ground is the Father’s kindness to the unthankful — which is precisely the argument the merit-based instinct in charity refuses.

expand to see more

Lend, hoping for nothing again. The command is given in the same breath as loving enemies and doing good, and the reason attached is that God is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil. Christian giving is therefore modelled on a kindness that its recipients have not earned and will not repay, which cuts against the instinct — strong and often dressed as prudence — to make help conditional on the recipient’s deserving. Scripture is not naive about this: it commands work (2 Thessalonians 3:10), warns against sloth throughout Proverbs, and expects wisdom in the exercise of mercy. But the wisdom governs the method, not the disposition, and a church whose giving is limited to the demonstrably deserving has adopted a standard by which it would itself have received nothing.

The Old Testament’s prohibition of usury to a poor brother has been the subject of long debate, and the Reformed tradition’s handling of it is worth stating. Calvin, examining Exodus 22:25 and its parallels, concluded that Scripture forbids the oppressive lending that exploits a brother’s need, not every charge for the productive use of capital, and the distinction has largely held in Protestant economic thought. What cannot be evaded is the text’s protective intent: the poor man is not a market. Deuteronomy 15:9 goes further and warns against the thought that rises in a wicked heart — that the year of release is at hand, and so the brother may be given nought. The calculation about repayment was accurate; the heart that let it govern a decision about need is what Scripture names.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lavah (H3867), to join, to borrow or lend; nashak (H5391), to bite, and so to lend on interest; Greek daneizo (G1155), to lend on interest; kichremi (G5531), to lend as a friendly act.

expand to see more

Hebrew lavah (H3867) — to join oneself to, and so to borrow or lend; the standing verb of Deuteronomy 15:8.

Hebrew nashak (H5391) — to bite; the same root gives neshek, interest, which bites the borrower (Exodus 22:25).

Hebrew chanan (H2603) — to show favour, to be gracious; the merciful lending of Psalm 37:26.

Greek daneizo (G1155) — to lend, ordinarily at interest; the verb Christ redefines in Luke 6:35.

Greek apelpizo (G560) — to give up hope of, to expect nothing back; hoping for nothing again (Luke 6:35).

Usage

"Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him (Deuteronomy 15:8) — lending to the poor as obligation, not opportunity."

"Thou shalt not be to him as an usurer (Exodus 22:25) — the poor man is not a market."

"Lend, hoping for nothing again... for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil (Luke 6:35) — the ground is the Father’s character."
